payload.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=longitudinal+preference+stability+in+multi-agent+reinforcement+learning+non-stationary+environments&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.4123080\", \"title\": [\"Context Detection and Identification in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning on Non-Stationary Environments\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Although the real world is non-stationary, most reinforcement learning algorithms are based on the assumption that the environment is stationary. Non-stationary environments are composed of several different stationary components (i.e., sub-environments or contexts). Therefore, algorithms that accept this assumption are incapable of learning within non-stationary environments. Reinforcement Learning - Context Detection (RL-CD) da Silva et al. (2016) method allows agents to learn the environment, detect context change points, and learn the partial model of the context without previous knowledge of the environment. RL-CD is a single-agent algorithm and it has shortcomings in learning within a multi-agent environment. In this work, we introduce a new method called Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning - Context Detection (MARL-CD), which can both detect context change points and enable agents to learn within non-stationary environments with multi-agent settings. This approach is based on RL-CD and works more effectively in terms of detecting context changes caused by agents and changes caused by the environment’s dynamics. It detects not only the change points originating from the environment, but also the change points created by the agents. Experimentally, agents spend 16% less energy compared to RL-CD and can detect change points more accurately and earlier.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4123080\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2022]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.70675/0c2168aaz74edz47a7z87b1z55403db85295\", \"title\": [\"Reinforcement learning in non-stationary environments\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:title>Apprentissage par renforcement en environement non stationnaire</jats:title>\\n                <jats:p xml:lang=\\\"fr\\\">Comment un agent doit-il agir étant donné que son environnement évolue de manièreincertaine ? Dans cette thèse, nous fournissons une réponse à cette question du point devue de l’apprentissage par renforcement. Le problème est vu sous trois aspects différents.Premièrement, nous étudions le compromis planification vs. re-planification des algorithmesde recherche arborescente dans les Processus Décisionnels Markoviens. Nous proposons uneméthode pour réduire la complexité de calcul d’un tel algorithme, tout en conservant desguaranties théoriques sur la performance. Deuxièmement, nous étudions le cas des environnementsévoluant graduellement au cours du temps. Cette hypothèse est formulée dansun cadre mathématique appelé Processus de Décision Markoviens Non-Stationnaires Lipschitziens.Dans ce cadre, nous proposons un algorithme de planification robuste aux évolutionspossibles, dont nous montrons qu’il converge vers la politique minmax. Troisièmement,nous considérons le cas de l’évolution temporelle abrupte dans le cadre du “lifelong learning”(apprentissage tout au long de la vie). Nous proposons une méthode de transfert non-négatifbasée sur l’étude théorique de la continuité de Lipschitz de la Q-fonction optimale par rapportà l’espace des tâches. L’approche permet d’accélérer l’apprentissage dans de nouvelles tâches.Dans l’ensemble, cette dissertation propose des réponses à la question de la résolution desProcessus de Décision Markoviens Non-Stationnaires dans trois cadres d’hypothèses.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.70675/0c2168aaz74edz47a7z87b1z55403db85295\"}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7404755\", \"title\": [\"Tracking Non-Stationary Equilibria in Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Evolutionary Dynamics\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Non-stationarity is a fundamental challenge in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). It arises from the continuous and simultaneous learning of multiple agents: as each agent adapts its policy, the environment dynamics change over time, continuously shifting the equilibria. This problem is further compounded when the learning dynamics themselves are inherently non-stationary. Evolutionary game theory (EGT) offers a complementary perspective on this challenge by studying how strategies evolve within a population over time. However, existing work combining EGT with MARL remains limited to simple, tabular settings, and consequently fails to exploit the scalability of deep reinforcement learning.We introduce Deep Evolutionary Dynamics (DeepED), a novel actor-critic MARL algorithm that integrates evolutionary game theory into deep reinforcement learning. Instead of directly optimising policies towards expected returns, DeepED leverages critic-based fitness estimates to generate an evolutionary target policy via evolutionary dynamics, and the actor policy is then updated to track this target.On the theoretical side, we establish a dynamical regret bound for DeepED. Furthermore, we prove that the value gap between the Nash value and the current expected value follows a contraction of a quadratic form.Beyond the theoretical analysis, we evaluate DeepED across three levels of progressively increasing complexity: matrix games, gridworld environments and VMAS tasks. Empirical results demonstrate that DeepED tracks shifting equilibria more accurately and stably than prominent baselines such as QMIX, MAPPO and IPPO. Ultimately, these results show that DeepED successfully extends evolutionary principles beyond simple games to challenging, high-dimensional settings.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7404755\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1109/cdc49753.2023.10384223\", \"title\": [\"Non-Stationary Policy Learning for Multi-Timescale Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1109/cdc49753.2023.10384223\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2023, 12, 13]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "4d835bc87a39e027835cda87b95ae1cf5ced978fddcac1e185d1dba251016647", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "emergent_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.4123080", "doi:10.70675/0c2168aaz74edz47a7z87b1z55403db85295", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7404755", "doi:10.1109/cdc49753.2023.10384223"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4123080", "https://doi.org/10.70675/0c2168aaz74edz47a7z87b1z55403db85295", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7404755", "https://doi.org/10.1109/cdc49753.2023.10384223"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

payload.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=autonomous+goal+formation+intrinsic+motivation+objective+discovery&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.20944/preprints202607.0905.v1\", \"title\": [\"Beyond Human-Designed Objectives: Autonomous Goal Generation in AI Through Intrinsic Motivation and Self-Directed Agency\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Current artificial intelligence systems remain fundamentally constrained by their dependence on human-designed objectives and reward functions, limiting their capacity for genuine autonomy and open-ended development. This paper proposes Autonomous Goal Generation Networks (AGGNs), a theoretical framework for architectures that synthesize, evaluate, and pursue their own objectives through intrinsic motivation. {"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=mechanisms+for+autonomous+identification+and+prioritization+of+research+gaps+in+open-ended+learning&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Large Language Models in Preclinical Spine Research: A Scoping Review and Expert Perspective on Evidence-Aware Experimental Workflows.\", \"abstract\": \"

Background

Preclinical spine research is limited by heterogeneous experimental reporting, fragmented documentation, and barriers to reproducibility and translational alignment. Large language models (LLMs) and related artificial intelligence (AI) technologies may support semantic interpretation, structured data extraction, and reasoning over biomedical text, but their role in experimental spine science remains unclear. This focused scoping review and expert perspective mapped current AI/LLM applications in spine research, quantified the preclinical evidence gap, and identified responsible integration opportunities.

Methods

A structured search of PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science was performed for studies published from January 2020 to January 2026 evaluating LLM, AI, chatbot, or advanced natural language processing applications in spine-related contexts. The search intentionally captured both LLM-specific and broader AI/chatbot applications to map the translational landscape. For this preclinical-focused analysis, the corpus was re-examined for experimental and translational use cases, supplemented by expert synthesis of methodologically relevant adjacent biomedical literature.

Results

Of 792 records identified, 166 unique studies met inclusion criteria. Publication activity increased markedly over time. The literature was dominated by conversational assessment/patient-reported outcome measure applications (82/166; 49.4%), patient education/information quality studies (53/166; 31.9%), and other LLM/AI applications (19/166; 11.4%). Preclinical/basic science applications were rare (3/166; 1.8%) and used classical machine learning, deep learning, or broader AI frameworks rather than generative LLMs. The most credible near-term opportunities include schema-constrained data extraction, protocol completeness checking, ontology-aligned data structuring, and evidence-grounded workflow support under human supervision.

Conclusion

In preclinical spine research, LLMs are best positioned as human-supervised workflow instruments for structuring fragmented experimental knowledge. Here, we systematically reviewed how large language models (LLMs) are being explored as support tools for adverse drug reaction (ADR) detection, extraction, triage, and documentation, highlighting their potential for precision medicine and big data-enabled safety monitoring. Methods: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines, we systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published between January 2022 and March 2026. Ultimately, 83 empirical studies satisfied the inclusion criteria. A narrative synthesis was conducted to address methodological heterogeneity across these studies. Results: LLM applications were concentrated in constrained information-extraction and classification tasks, including signal evaluation, clinical-note extraction, social media surveillance, and literature screening. Quantitative performance varied substantially by system design: error-correction prompting yielded an F1-score of 0.921 for ADR named entity recognition, whereas retrieval-augmented generation improved data-retrieval accuracy from 8.3% to 78.3%. Most studies were retrospective, benchmark-based, or proof-of-concept evaluations. Across 581 paired pre-consensus domain judgements, observed inter-rater agreement was 90.4% and Cohen's κ was 0.837 (95% CI 0.772-0.895). Hallucination, low specificity, prompt sensitivity, narrow datasets, and weak external validation remained common limitations. Conclusions: Current evidence supports supervised, task-specific applications of LLMs for extraction, triage, retrieval, and documentation rather than autonomous pharmacovigilance decision-making. qualitative exploration of rapid cycle deliberate practice effects on electrocardiographic monitoring judgment in critical cardiac care nurses.\", \"abstract\": \"

Background

Electrocardiographic interpretation competency among critical cardiac care nurses remains inadequate despite technological advances, creating patient safety concerns and alarm fatigue. Traditional nursing education utilizing didactic knowledge transmission has proven insufficient for developing time-critical electrocardiographic interpretation skills. Rapid cycle deliberate practice emerges as an innovative methodology integrating deliberate practice principles, immediate feedback, and psychologically safe environments through pause-coach-resume mechanisms.

Methods

Semi-structured interviews utilized Tanner's clinical judgment model as the questioning framework, supplemented by field observations. Interviews explored experiences around the noticing-interpreting-responding-reflecting continuum, with analysis conducted using NVivo software following van Manen's methodology.

Results

Four interconnected themes emerged: shifting perceptual focus from fragmented data perception toward holistic pattern recognition; shifting cognitive models from mechanical matching toward integrating intuition and evidence; evolving response patterns from hesitant reactivity toward confident proactivity; and redefined professional role encompassing new professional identity, ethical responsibility, and continuous learning commitment.

Conclusions

Analysis through Tanner's clinical judgment framework suggested perceived multidimensional shifts within critical cardiac care nurses' clinical judgment processes, as reflected in participants' descriptions of changes transcending technical skill acquisition to encompass reconceptualizations of clinical reasoning, professional identity, and ethical responsibility. Notably, the psychologically safe environment created through the pause-coach-resume mechanism appeared central to enabling these perceived shifts. These findings indicate that effective competency development requires educational approaches addressing cognitive, behavioral, and identity dimensions simultaneously, with implications for institutional integration of rapid cycle deliberate practice into staff development and future longitudinal investigation of its effectiveness.\", \"doi\": \"10.1371/journal.pone.0353168\", \"pmid\": \"42406754\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13336174\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0353168\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13336174\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13336174?pdf=render\"}]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "b25b751c65cd5b6c0dc3ca0502c07bd314c8356b645366b9e3c63e68555cb295", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unassigned_problem", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.1002/jsp2.70203", "doi:10.3390/diagnostics16152435", "doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0353168", "pmc:PMC13344227", "pmc:PMC13465311", "pmc:PMC13649983", "pmc:PMC13336174"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.1002/jsp2.70203", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13344227", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13344227?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.3390/diagnostics16152435", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13465311", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13465311?pdf=render", "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13649983/?tool=EBI", "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13649983/pdf/?tool=EBI"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
